To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
early childhood experiences can have a profound impact on health throughout life and that this effect is often mediated by epigenetic processes.

(1) the roots of adult disease are found among early biological and developmental disruptions; (2) there is often a lag between the early experience and the expression of disease; (3) early experiences can affect health in 2 different ways, by cumulative damage over the life course or by biological embedding of adversity in sensitive developmental periods; and (4) the effects of early adversity can be mitigated by the quality of the environment and relationships experienced during childhood.

the origins of many adult diseases are found in early life, and that early interventions are often the most effective and cost-efficient means of improving adult health and reducing health disparities.

the origins of adult health disparities, and we believe it is time to build a new scientific framework for health promotion, disease prevention, and health policy.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the early childhood roots of health inequalities are a critical issue that must be addressed if we are to make progress on health disparities.

(a) the roots of adult disease are found early in life; (b) early adversity can have long-term consequences for adult health, even when it occurs during sensitive developmental periods; (c) early adversity may be expressed as a cumulative effect over time; and (d) early adversity may have an impact on adult health by biological embedding of adverse experiences.

(i) early life experiences, particularly those involving social adversity, can have a significant impact on adult disease risk; (ii) the effects of these experiences are often mediated through biological mechanisms; (iii) there is a strong scientific basis for the hypothesis that early life experiences can have a cumulative impact on disease risk, with effects that can last a lifetime; and (iv) there are many potential opportunities to intervene to prevent or reduce disease risk, and to promote health and well-being in adulthood,

early experiences matter for later health.
the early years of childhood are the most important for health and development.

we must move away from a focus on the immediate causes of disease, such as smoking or lack of exercise, to the developmental and biological processes that underlie the health disparities we are seeing today.
we can do a much better job of improving the lives of all children by investing in the early years, and that we must take a broader view of what it means to be healthy.
